The fame had a cost. For decades, critics said he had too much influence. They said he saw the world only through European eyes, defended the liberal order as it was, and stayed too long. To some, the nation's conscience had become a nagging parent.

Then came one of his last public acts. After Hamas's attack on October 7, he co-signed a statement supporting Israel. It offered no support to Palestinian civilians. It also rejected the claim that Israel meant to commit genocide, the deliberate destruction of a people. Many people, even colleagues, read it as backing for more attacks. The reviewer himself calls Israel's response deadly on a genocidal scale. After Habermas died, critics piled on. Some even said he shared the guilt for mass murder.

The reviewer sees a deeper problem. Habermas's two most important books, from 1962 and 1981, both said the public sphere was breaking down. Money and political power, they argued, were pushing out real conversation. Yet for 70 years he wrote newspaper essays as if reasoned public debate still worked. His theory said the space was dying. His career assumed it was alive. He never explained how both could be true. He even called his public writing a mere side job.

The ending is bitter. Since his death, the reviewer says, the fights over his legacy read like angry posts on X. They chase likes. They show no wish to understand or to convince. His critics proved his darkest prediction right.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: Verovšek defends him. After 1945, nothing promised that Germany would become a stable democracy. Democracy there had to be "made, not found". Habermas did not just defend a working public sphere. He helped build it. The defeats of the last fifteen years do not erase that.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: His ideal of free, fair debate was easiest to see once it was gone.

recall.q: What contradiction does the reviewer find between Habermas's major books and his life as a public thinker?
recall.a: His 1962 and 1981 books said the public sphere was breaking down under money and political power. Yet for 70 years he wrote in newspapers as if reasoned public debate still worked, and he never explained how both could be true.

cards.title: Closed skies are shrinking where US military planes can fly
cards.body: Wars in Ukraine and Iran have closed large parts of the sky between Europe and Asia. The US military depends on the same civilian airspace, airports and airlines. Each route that closes makes the others more crowded and easier to break.

sections.text:
At one point, air traffic between Europe and Asia squeezed through a gap only about 160 kilometres wide. To the north is Russian airspace, closed to Western airlines since 2022. To the south are Iranian and Gulf airspace, disrupted by the 2026 Iran war. In between, Georgia, Azerbaijan, Armenia and Turkey now carry much of the traffic.

The US military has its own cargo planes. But it also relies on civilian airlines, airports and overflight rights. Overflight rights are a country's permission to fly through its sky. In 2009, Russia gave those rights to US military planes. By April 2011, more than 1,000 US supply missions had crossed Russia to reach Afghanistan. That route is now closed.

Even allies can say no. Spain refused to let US planes supporting attacks on Iran use its airspace and bases. Fifteen aircraft, most of them refuelling tankers, left Spain. At least seven moved to Ramstein in Germany.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: The losses stack up. After Russia closed, traffic moved south to the Caucasus and the Gulf. Then the Iran war hit the Gulf, and fewer backup routes were left. The US keeps a reserve of civilian planes it can call on for extra lift. But those planes cannot create overflight rights. As the head of US Transportation Command put it, America is now "fighting to move, instead of moving to fight."

sections.label: The details
items: Northern route lost: Finnair's Helsinki–Tokyo flight went from about 9 hours to 13. Chinese airlines kept Russian airspace, and their share of China–Europe flight capacity rose from 55% (2019) to 83% (2025).
Caucasus squeeze: Azerbaijan handled about 278 flights a day in early 2022, and 695 by the end of 2025.
Southern route hit: on 31 March 2026, flights between the Middle East and Europe were down 56%. Dubai's passenger numbers fell 31.3% in the first half of 2026.

Workaround: before the Iran war, the US moved about 150 military aircraft into Europe and the Middle East. More than half went to Europe, out of range of Iran's missiles. Tankers from Europe refuelled B-1 bombers over the Middle East.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Ukraine has asked ICAO, the UN's aviation body, to declare Russian airspace unsafe for civilian flights. Big cargo planes are also running short. Boeing stopped making the C-17 in 2015 and delivered its last 747 in 2023. An EU-funded study from September 2026 gives Europe two options: heavily upgrade Ukraine's An-124s, or build a new European plane to replace the C-17.

recall.q: Why did the Iran war's hit to Gulf routes hurt so much, and why can't extra civilian planes fix the problem?
recall.a: Western airlines had already lost Russian airspace in 2022, so traffic had moved south through the Caucasus and the Gulf. When the Gulf was hit too, few backup routes were left. Reserve civilian planes add carrying space, but they cannot create overflight rights, which are a country's permission to fly through its sky.
